 October 27, 2026 
 GOP, Dem trends to watch ahead of Election Day
 Happy Tuesday morning. Election Day is one week away.
 News: Speaker Mike Johnson will be in 13 states and 21 districts in the week leading up to Election Day. Johnson will be with Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) today. Johnson will then head to districts including AZ-06, IA-03, MI-10, NM-02, NY-03, NY-04, NC-01, OH-01, OH-09, PA-07, PA-10, VA-02 and WI-03.
 What we’re watching: One week out. Most Republicans and Democrats agree on one thing (at least privately) — Democrats will take control of the House. The size of that majority remains uncertain, however.
 But the Senate is up for grabs. Democrats see multiple paths to victory, although Republicans are pouring staggering amounts of money into close races in red states. Republicans are counting on that final blitz of TV ads to blunt the Democratic tide.
 Those are the toplines. Today we wanted to highlight a few trends you might be missing that will shape the midterms.
 How many House Democrats lose? Democrats are growing so confident in the final stretch that they think there’s a real chance they lose only one incumbent: Rep. Darren Soto of Florida. That would be a remarkable feat, given that the GOP redistricting push left a number of House Democrats in deep red seats.
 The most endangered Democrats are Soto and Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama. Yet Democratic leaders believe there’s still a chance Figures wins if Black voters turn out in significant numbers.
 The next tier: Democratic Reps. Vicente Gonzalez (Texas), Kathy Castor (Fla.), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.), Jared Moskowitz (Fla.), Don Davis (N.C.), Marcy Kaptur (Ohio) and Gabe Vasquez (N.M.).
 Besides those nine — all but two of whom were redistricted — no other Democratic incumbent seems to be in serious peril. Remember, GOP outside groups already gave up on ousting Reps. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas), Greg Landsman (D-Ohio), Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.) and Susie Lee (D-Nev.). They almost gave up on Moskowitz, as well.
 Spoiler alert. In the final stretch, super PACs aligned with both parties are quietly dumping millions of dollars to boost third-party spoilers.
 So far we’ve seen at least $7.2 million spread across 15 battleground races for control of the House and Senate. The vast majority of that is in Ohio. But some of the spending is sprinkled across other Senate contests in Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina, plus 10 House races.
 The investments are relatively modest compared to what both parties are spending for their nominees in marquee contests. Yet they have the potential to make a significant impact in close races. Liberal third-party candidates, such as those from the Green Party, pose the greatest risk to Democrats, while conservative third-party candidates, mainly Libertarians, could hurt the GOP.
 Ohio’s Senate race is seeing the most action, with $5.6 million in meddling. A group called Enough Promises Ohio spent $2.3 million to help socialist Greg Levy siphon votes from former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio). A group called Buckeye Freedom PAC spent $3.3 million promoting Libertarian Bill Redpath to hurt Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio).
 Outside Ohio, the next biggest player is a mysterious new group called Our Heritage Matters, which is spending $1.2 million so far to aid Democratic candidates in races including Montana’s open 1st District, Kentucky’s open 6th District, Iowa’s open 2nd District and in seats held by Reps. Mike Turner (R-Ohio) and Gabe Evans (R-Colo.). They’re also spending to help Gonzalez in Texas’ 34th District.
 On the GOP side, Progressive Champions PAC, a conservative group that meddled in the Democratic primary to face Lawler, is back. This time, the group is boosting liberal third-party candidates in order to hurt the Democrats trying to oust Reps. Jen Kiggans (R-Va.) and Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.).
 Two other groups of note: Hawkeye Liberty PAC has spent $124,000 on mail and texts boosting Libertarian Thomas Laehn in Iowa’s Senate race. Laehn could pull votes from Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa).
 And Nevadans for Sensible Government has started spending small amounts to boost independent Lynn Chapman in an open Nevada district where Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson is running against Republican David Flippo. This was one of the districts where the DCCC signaled to outside groups that it wanted help boosting these third-party candidates. Pop-up super PACs made a difference by helping minor party candidates in some key races in 2024.
 Governors. The top-of-the-ticket races in Iowa, Ohio, Michigan and Texas could play a role in those states’ toss-up Senate contests.
 In Iowa, Republicans are heartened that GOP gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn may be closing the gap on Democrat Rob Sand, providing the GOP with optimism that Hinson could pull out a victory in the Senate race. Sand is still heavily favored to win, but Republicans feel that the polling gap is getting somewhat better.
 In Michigan and Texas, the fortunes of Rep. John James (R-Mich.) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott could boost former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s chances. Conversely, in Ohio, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s floundering campaign may drag on Husted.
 Republican chances in these Senate races in Trump-won states will hinge on whether undecided MAGA voters come home to GOP candidates. Keep an eye on gubernatorial races for signs of whether the Republican base voters are doing so.
 - Ally Mutnick , Jake Sherman , Max Cohen
